solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pieces of paper needed for this? Not right

definitions.text: Pieces of paper needed for this? Not right

parts.words: Pieces of paper needed for this? Not right
parts.note: a paper print-out is the hard version of a document; the version needing no paper is its opposite, and PAPER without its R splits as P (soft, in music) and APE (copy)

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about whether paper is required for some task, followed by a curt correction.
explanation.walkthrough: A further layer: PAPER 'not right' loses its R to leave P + APE, and P is the musical mark for soft while APE means copy.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic document on screen is the opposite of a printed one, so no sheets of paper are needed for it.

clue.text: Firm with courier arrangements

parts.note: firm, as in solid or fixed, means set
UPS is a well-known parcel courier company

explanation.surface: A company teams up with a delivery service to make its plans.
explanation.definitionFit: Configurations or organised layouts of equipment or people are what this hyphenated word names.

clue.text: Football team favouring set plays

parts.note: to be for something is to favour it

indicators.note: the letters of 'set' play about, being rearranged

explanation.surface: A football side that prefers to score from rehearsed set pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plays' makes EST from SET. Nottingham Forest is an English football club, usually just called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Nottingham Forest, a famous English club, is commonly known by its second word alone.

clue.text: Pardon setter — a good anagram's first in a bit

indicators.note: in tells us the group of letters goes inside the coin

parts.note: a bit is an old name for a small coin, as in a threepenny bit
the crossword setter refers to themself as me

indicators.note: first takes only the opening letter of the word anagram

explanation.surface: The setter apologises, admitting a good anagram came first briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pardon' looks like an apology but is the request to repeat something. MEAGA goes inside COIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are polite requests asking a speaker to repeat what they just said.

clue.text: May Heath Robinson provide examples of these peculiar machines? Some, initially

definitions.text: May Heath Robinson provide examples of these peculiar machines? Some, initially

parts.words: May Heath Robinson provide examples of these peculiar machines? Some, initially
parts.note: Theresa May and Edward Heath held Britain's top political office, and the opening letters of peculiar machines and Some spell the usual abbreviation PMS

explanation.surface: Wondering whether cartoonist Heath Robinson might draw some of his famously contraptions.
explanation.walkthrough: Heath Robinson was a British cartoonist of absurdly elaborate machines, but here May and Heath are two separate British leaders.
explanation.definitionFit: Theresa May and Edward Heath both led UK governments, so each is an example of a British head of government.

clue.text: Not the ultimate second-class form of money

indicators.note: the last letter is dropped, and it must be the one matching the second

parts.note: a species is a class or kind of thing

explanation.surface: Something not quite top-class is called a second-rate form of currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second-class' looks like one adjective, but splits into S and the synonym for class.
explanation.definitionFit: Coins rather than banknotes are called this, money in metal form.

clue.text: Song Paul Simon composed — no No.1, you said

indicators.note: composed signals that the letters of Paul Simon are rearranged, with 'no' saying some of them are left over

parts.note: No. is the abbreviation for number, letters N and O
1 as a Roman numeral is I

indicators.note: said signals a letter that sounds like the word you

parts.note: the word you is taken as written and spoken, giving the letter that sounds the same

explanation.surface: Paul Simon wrote a song that wasn't a chart-topper, as you mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges PAULSIMON, and 'no' says the letters N, O, I and U are not used, leaving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacred song or hymn, especially from the Bible's book of them, is what this word means.

clue.text: A large number try and fail somehow, in a cunningly deceptive way

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100, a large number

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of try and fail end up in some other order

explanation.surface: Many people attempt something and fail, all while being sneaky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' turns TRY and FAIL into RAFTILY.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb describes acting with cunning and slyness, in a deceitful manner.

clue.text: Work out tax required, without hesitation

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the tax goes round the hesitation

parts.note: excise is a tax on goods
er is the sound of hesitating

explanation.surface: Calculate a tax bill without dithering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work out' reads as calculate, but means physical training. 'without' means outside here, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical training or a workout is a session of this, and to work out means to train the body.

clue.text: "Do behave!" "Two of us are married in this threesome" (parts of speech)

definitions.text: "Do behave!" "Two of us are married in this threesome" (parts of speech)

parts.words: "Do behave!" "Two of us are married in this threesome" (parts of speech)
parts.note: do, be and have are the three helping verbs of English grammar; in the word behave two of them are joined together

explanation.surface: A scolding, then a racy confession about a married couple in a threesome.
explanation.walkthrough: The threesome is DO, BE and HAVE; 'behave' marries BE and HAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Do, be and have are the helping verbs of English, used with main verbs to form tenses and questions.

clue.text: Which doctors ignored case for home birth? Clots!

indicators.note: doctors as a verb means tampers with, rearranging the letters
the outer letters of home, its case, are dropped and only the inside kept

explanation.surface: An indignant question about doctors who dismissed a home birth, ending in an insult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doctors' looks like a noun but is the verb; OM plus BIRTH becomes the answer. 'Clots!' looks like an insult but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Blood clots in a vessel are known in medicine by this Latin plural.

clue.text: Ignorant female facing conflict online

parts.note: Una is a woman's name
war is armed conflict
E stands for electronic, as in e-mail, so online

explanation.surface: A woman unaware of things, confronting a fight on the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: Not knowing about something, lacking knowledge of it, is the sense here.

clue.text: Old man has upset former Turkish officer

parts.note: old man is slang for father, pa

indicators.note: upset means the letters of has are knocked over into a new order

explanation.surface: An elderly man is distressed by an ex-Ottoman officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns HAS into SHA.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the title of a high-ranking official or military commander in the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Puzzling time in charge, unevenly managed

indicators.note: managed suggests the letters are handled and arranged afresh
unevenly picks the odd-numbered letters of charge

explanation.surface: A spell in charge, run erratically, that baffles observers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unevenly' gives CAG from 'charge'; with TIME and IN, 'managed' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: Mysterious and hard to interpret, like a riddle, is what this adjective conveys.

clue.text: On St David's Day, iffy palmist entertains English group having its ups and downs in Europe

definitions.text: group having its ups and downs in Europe

parts.note: St David's Day, the Welsh national day, falls on 1 March, so Mar 1

indicators.note: entertains means holds inside, taking in another letter
iffy means dubious, so the letters of palmist come out in a doubtful order

explanation.surface: On Wales's patron saint's day, a dubious palm-reader hosts an English party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'iffy' rearranges PALMIST as TIMALPS, which 'entertains' E. St David is the patron saint of Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A mountain range is a group whose peaks rise and fall, and this one sits on the French-Italian border.

clue.text: Roving eye? Flirt admits heading for cheap thrill

indicators.note: admits means lets in, taking a letter inside
roving means wandering, so the letters wander out of order
heading for picks the first letter of cheap

explanation.surface: A flirt with a wandering eye seeks a cheap thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roving' makes ELETRIFY from EYE and FLIRT, which 'admits' C.
explanation.definitionFit: To excite someone intensely, as though with an electric charge, is to thrill them.

clue.text: Some calm water philosopher thought about deeply? Not half!

parts.note: John Stuart Mill was a British philosopher

indicators.note: not half says only half of the word is kept, dropping the rest

parts.note: pondered means thought about deeply

explanation.surface: A philosopher's deep thoughts on still water, answered with an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', but here it removes the second half of PONDERED.
explanation.definitionFit: A pond serving a watermill is proverbially still, hence the phrase for perfectly calm water.

clue.text: Small capitals current in poor quality writing

parts.note: SC is the printers' abbreviation for small capitals, small caps
a river is a current of water, and the Ribble is a river in north-west England

explanation.surface: Printing in small capitals is found in shoddy writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small capitals' looks like a typographical term but splits into S and C. The Ribble is a river in Lancashire.
explanation.definitionFit: Careless, hurried handwriting is a scrawl, the noun sense here.

clue.text: Explosive devices incorporated in French journals?

parts.note: en is the French for in
diaries are personal journals

explanation.surface: Bombs reported in French newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: Firebombs designed to start fires are explosive weapons called by this plural.

clue.text: Small trees destroyed by a bison

indicators.note: destroyed means the letters of a bison are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A bison tramples some little trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Miniature trees grown in pots using a Japanese art form are what this word names.

clue.text: Ill humour observed, consuming discontented chum

indicators.note: consuming means swallowing up something inside

parts.note: seen means observed

indicators.note: discontented means emptied of contents, the middle letter dropped

parts.note: pal is a word for a chum

explanation.surface: Bad temper is noticed, eating up an unhappy friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discontented' looks like it means unhappy, but it empties the friend of its middle letter. 'consuming' puts that inside the word for observed.
explanation.definitionFit: In old medicine the organ was the seat of bad temper, so it stands for spite or ill temper.

clue.text: The sound of fairgrounds: pointless theme

indicators.note: pointless removes a point of the compass, here E for east
the sound of says we need words that sound like light and motive

parts.note: fair can mean light, as in fair hair, and grounds means motive

explanation.surface: The noise of funfairs is a tiresome recurring motif.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fairgrounds' splits as FAIR (light) and GROUNDS (motive); spoken they give a German-looking word, and 'pointless' drops its E.
explanation.definitionFit: A recurring musical or literary motif associated with a character or idea is this German-derived term.

clue.text: Joint area of responsibility when cycling around

indicators.note: cycling around moves the letters round, the front ones going to the back

parts.note: a remit is one's area of responsibility

explanation.surface: A shared area of responsibility while riding bikes around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling around' moves RE from the front of REMIT to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworking joint made at an angle, as in picture frames, is this type.

clue.text: Soldiers' wretched time, retreating

definitions.note: read as soldiers is, a body of soldiers

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: poor means wretched

explanation.surface: Soldiers have a miserable time while falling back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreating' reverses POORT. 'Soldiers'' reads as 'soldiers is', joined to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A company of soldiers, especially cavalry, is a unit of this name.

clue.text: Perhaps satellite organisation has small part for middle daughter

indicators.note: for means in place of, one piece replacing another

parts.note: an order is an organisation, like a religious order
the D in the middle of the word, D being the abbreviation for daughter
a bit is a small part

explanation.surface: An organisation gives a minor role to a middle child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' says a satellite is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A satellite circles a planet, and anything in orbit is so called, a satellite being one example.

clue.text: Put out again by note written by children

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
issue means offspring, children

explanation.surface: Republished a memo written by the kids.
explanation.definitionFit: To publish or release a second time, such as a book or record, is the sense here.

clue.text: German male who's trying to lose weight?

definitions.meaning: a common German man's first name
a person on a slimming regime

explanation.surface: A German man attempting to slim down.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a German first name and also a slimmer who follows a restricted eating plan.

clue.text: Fool Year 1 with an Aramaic dialect

parts.note: an ass is a fool
1 as a Roman numeral is I

explanation.surface: A silly first-year pupil speaks an ancient Semitic tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Year 1' looks like a school class but splits into YR and I.
explanation.definitionFit: The language of the ancient Mesopotamian empire is a related dialect still spoken by Christian communities.
